title: Norwood Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Norwood wells have a 126 ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,200-$24,600 in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Norwood, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Norwood means understanding the ground below the lot, not just the view or road access. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 126 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 40 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for budgeting, but they are not a guarantee for one parcel. Most local permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, where water can vary sharply from one location to the next. Check nearby well records, confirm the intended use, and have a driller evaluate access before you commit to a building plan.

sections.heading: Norwood’s well depths reflect fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Norwood is 126 feet. The middle half runs from 60 to 250 feet, so a bid based only on the median can be misleading. The 90th-percentile depth is 330 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 850 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 40% are under 100 feet, 42% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 17% reach 300 to 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The local permits mostly name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 489 wells in that category. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures rather than a uniform underground layer, so neighboring wells are valuable evidence but not a promise.

sections.heading: A 7.0 gpm median is a workable starting point
sections.html:
Reported well yield has a median of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a useful range for a household, but storage and pump design still matter, especially if irrigation or stock water is part of the plan.

Only 65 wells report a pump yield, so the yield data is not complete for all permitted wells. Six percent of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, 25% produce 1 to 5, 48% produce 5 to 15, and 22% produce 15 or more. Ask for the well completion report and pumping test rather than relying on a nearby well’s result.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels are not showing a simple decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 40 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 20 to 90 feet. Static water level means the water level when the well is not being pumped; it is not the same as well depth or guaranteed available supply.

The decade series does not suggest a dropping table in these records. The median measured level was 52 feet below ground in the 2010s and 40 feet in the 2020s, meaning the more recent median is shallower. Only 31 wells report a static water level, however, so this should be treated as limited local evidence rather than a basin-wide trend. A driller can check the site and nearby logs for a better comparison.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady local drilling through 2025
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 520 permitted wells within the Norwood search area, including 324 recorded as constructed. The newest permit year is 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 1990s and 2000s, with 120 and 124 permits respectively. There were 39 permits in the 2010s and 33 in the 2020s.

The most active names in the records are Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.) with 67 wells, Gordon Smith And Company (Smith, Gordon R.) with 42, and Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth) with 35. These records show who has worked in the area; confirm current licensing, availability, insurance, and the exact scope of a new-well proposal before hiring.

sections.heading: Norwood drilling costs rise quickly with depth
sections.html:
Norwood’s fractured granite and gneiss make depth the main cost variable. The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 126 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,200 to $12,600.

A finished well is more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled total at the median depth is about $14,200 to $24,600. A deeper-than-typical hole can push the price higher, and difficult access, casing, grout, water testing, or a dry hole may be handled separately. Get a written bid that says what happens if the first target depth does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic space, and low-yield risk
sections.html:
Water quality deserves its own investigation. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 5 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped data, but that does not make an individual well automatically safe. Test the water after construction and review the site history, especially near mining activity.

Low yield and dry holes are practical risks in fractured rock. Confirm the intended household use with Colorado DWR before drilling; an exempt household-use well is subject to its permit terms and the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Leave enough workable area for a septic system, replacement area, driveway, and building setbacks. Septic placement and well protection need to be planned together.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Norwood lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare permitted wells in Norwood and nearby Redvale, which is 7 miles away. Naturita and Placerville are each 16 miles away, while Nucla is 17 miles away. Those surrounding records can help a driller understand the broader rock setting, but the closest wells should carry the most weight.

Before closing, ask for every existing well permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality result, and repair record. For an undeveloped lot, obtain a site-specific drilling estimate and verify rig access, electrical service, trench length, and septic feasibility. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement affects the proposed use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Norwood, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Norwood is 126 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 60 to 250 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 330 feet. Forty percent are under 100 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock can produce much deeper wells, including one recorded at 850 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Norwood?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 126-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,200 to $12,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $14,200 to $24,600. Deeper drilling, difficult access, and nonproductive drilling can increase the final cost.

faq.q: How much water do Norwood wells produce?
faq.a: Reported well yield has a 7.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half between 3.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Six percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute. Because only 65 wells report a pump yield, request the specific well’s completion report and pumping test before relying on a nearby result.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Norwood?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. The mapped area includes 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 5 historic mine features, although there are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or newly completed well for relevant contaminants, and review nearby mining and property history before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are Norwood wells getting deeper or running dry?
faq.a: The available records do not show a simple declining water-level trend. Median static water level was 52 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 40 feet in the 2020s, which is shallower in the newer records. Only 31 wells report static water levels, so inspect the specific parcel and nearby well logs rather than assuming a dry-well risk is absent.
